fixes.explanation: Not quite, friend. The serpent asks, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’” but that's his question, not her answer. The woman answers, “We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden…” and then she points to one tree in the middle. Her answer has a whole lot more yes in it than his question did.

Yes. The woman says God has said, “You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.” Die is the word she uses for what would happen. She doesn't reach for anything softer. She puts it plainly to the serpent.

That's it. The serpent tells her, “You will not surely die…” She has just told him that God said they would die, and his answer is a flat contradiction. No warm-up and no hedging, just a smooth NO. Then he keeps talking, this time about what God knows (Genesis 3:5).
Yes. The serpent says, “…you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” Not like angels, not like kings. Like God. That's not a small offer, friend, and it comes straight from the serpent's mouth.

Yes. The text says “…they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.” Sewing leaves together, friend. That's real craftwork. My mustache can pack a cookie box all day, but I wouldn't trust it with a sewing job.

Yes. The text says they “…hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.” First they heard His voice walking in the garden, and then they went in among the trees. I think that's a heavy kind of hiding. The text says it plainly.

Nothing in his answer is about work, friend. He tells God, “I heard Your voice in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.” Afraid and naked are the two things he gives as his reason. Busy never comes up. If he'd said busy, that would be a whole different verse.

Yes. The LORD God says to the serpent, “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.” The head that gets crushed is the serpent's, since God is speaking to the serpent. The one doing the crushing comes from the woman's side of that line. The serpent's part in the verse is the strike to the heel.

Close, but it's turned around. The LORD God says to the serpent, “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.” Your head is the serpent's head, because God is speaking to the serpent. The strike to the heel is what the serpent does. Read those pronouns slowly, baker, and the picture comes clear.

Yes. The LORD God says Adam will return to the ground “because out of it were you taken.” Then He says, “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.” Dust is the word He uses for what Adam is. It's a heavy line, and the text just says it plainly.

That's right, baker. The man doesn't stay in the garden. The text says the LORD God “banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.” Just before that, the LORD God spoke of the man reaching out his hand to the tree of life and living forever (Genesis 3:22). I think this part of the story hurts.

Yes. The text says He “stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.” Cherubim and a whirling sword of flame are the answer. They're posted on the east side, and what they guard is the way to the tree of life. The text tells us exactly that.

North sounds sensible, baker, but the text says something else. He “stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden…” The guards stand on the east side, along with the whirling sword of flame. So turn that compass a quarter turn. North can sit this one out.
